Morning briefing in 3 commands: jarvis init --preset morning-digest-mac --force   (or -linux / -minimal) jarvis connect gdrive   (one Google sign-in covers Gmail, Calendar, Tasks) jarvis digest --fresh   (or just say "good morning" in the chat) If jarvis isn't found, put uv run in front of it. Heads up: - The spoken briefing uses a Cartesia or OpenAI API key (paid). Free: jarvis digest --text-only to read it (a local open source Kokoro voice is also in the code). - Gmail needs your own Google OAuth client (client_id:client_secret), the docs walk you through it. - Models run locally through Ollama, so your computer has to handle a local model. Cloud models are optional. - The installer asks about anonymous analytics - answer N if you don't want it. - The 40 emails in the video are an example, not a test result. building jarvis in your pocket This is exactly how I did it, no gatekeeping. I wanted a way to talk to my local Hermes agent quickly and easily. I’ll share my entire local AI setup with Hermes and my Second Brain soon, but in short my Hermes agent bounces between Qwen 3.8 27b for easy stuff, and GPT OSS 120b for more complex tasks. But realistically you can do this with any model that’s capable of handling simple queries. I purchased an M5Stack Stopwatch which is essentially a tiny computer built on the ESP32-S3 chip. It already has Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and a motion sensor in it, all packed into a round AMOLED stopwatch. All it needs, is a firmware. When I was originally trying to get one of these, they were all coming directly from China, which would take weeks. Fortunately I found that DigiKey had stock of them and I was able to get my hands on it much quicker. From there, I gave Claude Code the following prompt to build the firmware and Hermes plugin: “Build a Hermes plugin and ESP32 firmware so I can chat with my Hermes agent from a little pet on my esp32’s screen over local Wi-Fi. Keep it simple and walk me through it.” But this only worked if you and your device were on the same local Wi-Fi network. So I built in a redundant direct Bluetooth connection using this prompt: “Add Bluetooth as a backup. If the pet can’t reach Hermes over Wi-Fi, have it switch to Bluetooth LE with my PC automatically, and switch back to Wi-Fi when it’s available again.” Then finally, I wanted to be able to access it from anywhere so I built in a Tailscale option that I can flip on whenever I’m away from my Hermes computer (like the personal AI server I’m building) using this prompt: “Add Tailscale so the pet can reach Hermes from any Wi-Fi, not just my home network. Put it behind an on/off switch in the pet’s settings and keep my local Wi-Fi setup working as before.” I strongly encourage you to try things out like this. The first draft looked like every AI site, so: the free frontend-design plugin + "make it look premium" + 6 AI photos. 4. The database: Supabase, running on your own computer first. Publishable key in the browser, secret key only on the server. 5. The rule: anyone can read a published menu, only the owner can edit it. Put it in the database, then make the AI prove it with a second owner. It tried 24 ways. All failed. 6. Customer side: the public menu + a QR code that holds a permanent link. 7. Payments: a Stripe sandbox, $9/month, a webhook unlocks the account. 4242 unlocks, the decline card stays locked, fake "she paid" messages get refused. 8. Photos, then a security review before launch: nothing critical, 13 real problems, 11 fixed. 9. Online: GitHub (private), Vercel (Pro, because taking payments is commercial use), the online Supabase project, your domain. The 3 things that break on launch day: login emails (use Resend), login links pointing to localhost (set the site URL), and live Stripe keys + a new webhook.
